title: Crizotinib monotherapy

agents.name: Crizotinib
agents.type: Oral targeted therapy: ALK/ROS1 tyrosine kinase inhibitor
agents.mechanism: Blocks growth signals from abnormal ALK or ROS1 proteins
agents.explanation: An ALK or ROS1 rearrangement can drive cancer growth. Crizotinib blocks these signals in suitable cancers. It can also affect healthy tissues, so regular tests and symptom reporting remain important.
visual: Validated ALK or ROS1 tumour test
agents.watch: Report changes in breathing, vision, heartbeat, swelling, liver symptoms or severe bowel symptoms promptly. Check all other medicines before starting or changing them.
risks: Vision changes, sometimes severe visual loss
Nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea or constipation; appetite change
Liver injury, which can be serious or fatal
Lung inflammation (ILD/pneumonitis), which can be serious or fatal
Slow heart rate, abnormal heart rhythm and heart failure
Skin rash and sensitivity to sunlight
Potential harm to a pregnancy; fertility may be affected

questions.q: How long will I take treatment?
questions.a: The usual adult starting dose is 250 mg twice daily, every day, with no planned rest week. Use the strength and frequency on your own prescription. Treatment continues while it helps and side effects remain acceptable; there is no fixed course length.

questions.q: What if I miss a dose or vomit?
questions.a: Swallow 200 mg/250 mg hard capsules whole with water, with or without food; do not crush, dissolve or open them. Other formulations have different instructions. If a dose is missed, take it when remembered only if the next dose is at least 6 hours away; otherwise skip it. Never double a dose. If you vomit after a dose, do not take an extra dose; take the next dose at its usual time.

questions.q: Which checks happen most often at the start?
questions.a: Before starting: confirm the tumour test, blood count, kidney/liver tests, chest imaging, symptoms and all medicines; ECG and electrolytes near the first dose. Liver tests are planned weekly for the first 2 months using current product information, then monthly; NCCP says every 2 weeks initially, so confirm the local plan. Blood count and kidney tests are monthly. ECG, electrolytes, pulse and blood pressure need a planned schedule and earlier review if unwell. NCCP lists monthly chest X-ray; other disease imaging follows your consultant plan.

questions.q: Do I need to enter dates?
questions.a: No. This map gives general milestones. Your team books actual appointments and authorises treatment changes.

questions.q: Why does my nausea plan need checking?
questions.a: Crizotinib has moderate-to-high oral sickness risk. Agree daily prevention and rescue treatment with your team. The chosen medicine must account for heart-rhythm and drug-interaction risks; do not add anti-sickness medicines or a prolonged steroid course yourself.

questions.q: Do side effects mean it is working?
questions.a: Side effects do not show whether cancer is responding. The team uses symptoms, examinations, imaging and other planned tests to assess benefit.

In separate ALK studies, crizotinib delayed progression compared with the chemotherapy used at that time. The ROS1 study showed cancer responses but had no comparison group. These studies involve different populations and cannot rank present-day medicines or predict an individual outcome. Ask how the evidence fits your tumour, previous therapy, brain involvement and current alternatives.

timeline_note: Milestones show the order of care; symptoms can occur at any time.
safety_note: Follow your unit’s urgent contact plan. Serious illness can occur without fever; call for sudden illness.
teachback: Can you explain your capsule strength and frequency, the 6-hour missed-dose rule, the next liver test, medicines to check, and when to call urgently?
consent_support: Discuss the selected ALK/ROS1 indication and treatment line, individual aim and uncertainty, alternatives including not proceeding, material and lasting risks, interactions, fertility/pregnancy/feeding, daily treatment burden, monitoring, and your right to reconsider. This discussion aid is not consent or treatment authorisation.
urgent_extra: Contact your oncology team immediately for new or worsening breathlessness or cough, fainting, palpitations, severe dizziness, rapidly increasing swelling/weight, sudden or severe loss of vision, yellow skin/eyes, dark urine, fever/shivering or sudden illness, severe abdominal pain, or persistent vomiting/diarrhoea with poor drinking or little urine. Do not wait for the next appointment. Severe breathing difficulty, collapse or severe chest pain needs emergency help.

chapters.title: Your treatment and its purpose
chapters.intro: Crizotinib targets abnormal ALK or ROS1 signalling in selected advanced non-small-cell lung cancers. The aim is to control cancer and delay progression; the choice depends on the tumour test, previous treatment, other options and your priorities.

items.title: Confirm your indication
items.text: Adults with advanced ALK-positive or ROS1-positive NSCLC. NCCP 00243a is previously treated ALK disease; 00243b is ROS1 disease; 00243c is first-line ALK disease. Confirm the exact indication and local access; a listed indication, licence and reimbursement are different facts. This guide does not cover paediatric lymphoma or inflammatory myofibroblastic tumour.

items.title: Duration and review
items.text: The usual adult starting dose is 250 mg twice daily, every day, with no planned rest week. Use the strength and frequency on your own prescription. Treatment continues while it helps and side effects remain acceptable; there is no fixed course length.

chapters.title: Taking crizotinib at home
chapters.intro: The prescription and capsule formulation determine how you take it.

items.title: Taking, missing or vomiting a dose
items.text: Swallow 200 mg/250 mg hard capsules whole with water, with or without food; do not crush, dissolve or open them. Other formulations have different instructions. If a dose is missed, take it when remembered only if the next dose is at least 6 hours away; otherwise skip it. Never double a dose. If you vomit after a dose, do not take an extra dose; take the next dose at its usual time.

items.title: When a dose changes
items.text: A dose may change from twice daily to once daily. Ask for a written strength-and-frequency plan. Do not combine old and new instructions, add missed doses or restart after a clinical hold without advice.

chapters.title: Tests and symptom reviews
chapters.intro: Baseline checks and ongoing monitoring do different jobs.

items.title: Monitoring plan
items.text: Before starting: confirm the tumour test, blood count, kidney/liver tests, chest imaging, symptoms and all medicines; ECG and electrolytes near the first dose. Liver tests are planned weekly for the first 2 months using current product information, then monthly; NCCP says every 2 weeks initially, so confirm the local plan. Blood count and kidney tests are monthly. ECG, electrolytes, pulse and blood pressure need a planned schedule and earlier review if unwell. NCCP lists monthly chest X-ray; other disease imaging follows your consultant plan.

items.title: Eyes and breathing
items.text: Tell your team about visual symptoms and any new cough or breathlessness. Persistent or worsening vision problems need an eye assessment; severe visual loss needs urgent review. The routine paediatric eye-examination timetable does not apply automatically to adult NSCLC.

chapters.title: Support during treatment
chapters.intro: Ask for help with eating, fatigue, travel, work and emotional wellbeing.

items.title: A tailored anti-sickness plan
items.text: Crizotinib has moderate-to-high oral sickness risk. Agree daily prevention and rescue treatment with your team. The chosen medicine must account for heart-rhythm and drug-interaction risks; do not add anti-sickness medicines or a prolonged steroid course yourself.

items.title: Food and medicine interactions
items.text: Avoid grapefruit/grapefruit juice and St John’s wort. Check prescription medicines, pharmacy medicines, vitamins and herbal products before taking them. Some antibiotics, antifungals, heart medicines and seizure treatments interact. Do not stop a prescribed medicine without a plan.

items.title: Doses and supply
items.text: Swallow 200 mg/250 mg hard capsules whole with water, with or without food; do not crush, dissolve or open them. Other formulations have different instructions. If a dose is missed, take it when remembered only if the next dose is at least 6 hours away; otherwise skip it. Never double a dose. If you vomit after a dose, do not take an extra dose; take the next dose at its usual time. Request repeat supply early and keep a current medicines list. A clinician-held dose needs clinician authorisation to restart.

items.title: Pregnancy, fertility and feeding
items.text: Discuss fertility preservation before treatment. Use an effective agreed contraception plan during treatment and for at least 90 days after the last dose; this applies to men and women. Oral contraceptives may be less effective. Tell the team promptly about pregnancy and avoid breastfeeding during treatment.

items.title: Vision, driving and sunlight
items.text: Report visual changes. Take care with driving or machinery if vision, dizziness or fatigue affects safety. Avoid prolonged sun exposure and use protective clothing and sunscreen.

chapters.title: Symptoms that need prompt help
chapters.intro: Keep the oncology contact number available day and night.

items.title: Do not wait for the next visit
items.text: Contact your oncology team immediately for new or worsening breathlessness or cough, fainting, palpitations, severe dizziness, rapidly increasing swelling/weight, sudden or severe loss of vision, yellow skin/eyes, dark urine, fever/shivering or sudden illness, severe abdominal pain, or persistent vomiting/diarrhoea with poor drinking or little urine. Do not wait for the next appointment. Severe breathing difficulty, collapse or severe chest pain needs emergency help.

items.title: When you call
items.text: Give the medicine name, when the last dose was taken, what has changed, and whether you can drink and pass urine. Do not delay a call to collect details.

chapters.title: Discuss benefit and choices
chapters.intro: In separate ALK studies, crizotinib delayed progression compared with the chemotherapy used at that time. The ROS1 study showed cancer responses but had no comparison group. These studies involve different populations and cannot rank present-day medicines or predict an individual outcome. Ask how the evidence fits your tumour, previous therapy, brain involvement and current alternatives.

items.title: Evidence depends on the setting
items.text: ALK first-line, ALK after previous treatment and ROS1 disease were studied separately. The chemotherapy comparisons are historical; the ROS1 study was small and had no control group. Ask about the alternatives suitable for you, including supportive care and choosing not to proceed.

items.title: A change in the plan
items.text: Reviews consider symptoms, tests, cancer response, side effects and your priorities. Ask who will arrange follow-up and how to report symptoms after treatment stops. You may reconsider your consent.

evidence.title: ALK and ROS1 evidence: different study populations
evidence.intro: Study results describe groups and cannot predict an individual outcome.
evidence.population: Adults with advanced ALK-positive disease studied separately before/after prior therapy; a separate small ROS1 cohort.
evidence.comparison_label: Historical chemotherapy in ALK studies; no control in ROS1 cohort
evidence.interpretation: In separate ALK studies, crizotinib delayed progression compared with the chemotherapy used at that time. The ROS1 study showed cancer responses but had no comparison group. These studies involve different populations and cannot rank present-day medicines or predict an individual outcome. Ask how the evidence fits your tumour, previous therapy, brain involvement and current alternatives.
evidence.limitations: No cross-trial ranking or individual survival estimate. Confirm contemporary options with the team.

anatomy: Report visual change; severe visual loss needs urgent assessment.
Slow pulse, rhythm changes or fluid-related swelling need assessment.
New cough or breathlessness can indicate serious lung inflammation.
Liver tests and prompt reporting of jaundice or dark urine protect against serious injury.
Nausea, vomiting, bowel changes and severe abdominal pain need advice.
Report poor drinking or reduced urine; kidney tests continue during treatment.
Rash and sun sensitivity can occur; use protection and report severe changes.
